title: A negative-binomial model beat a fixed-mean zero-inflated Poisson model for late counts after 323 shallow M6.5+ earthquakes in 2013-2024
abstract: We tested whether a separate zero-event probability explains a published negative-binomial count score gain. We used a fixed ComCat snapshot, 363 training centers in 2001-2012 and 323 test centers in 2013-2024. Centers have M6.5 or more and depth at most 70 km. Targets are M5.5+ counts on days 7-30 within 200 km. A negative-binomial model beat a zero-inflated Poisson model at the same predicted mean by 0.1547 nats per center. The conditional 95% three-year block interval was 0.0424 to 0.3333. The positive-count score part supplied 97.1% of the point gain. The binary occurrence part was small and uncertain. All four planned secondary comparisons favored negative binomial under the same resampling scheme. This supports extra positive-count variation as a useful description in these model families. It does not identify a physical mechanism. The test data overlap prior work, and revised records, shared windows, fixed fits and twelve test years limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, a figure and a separate numerical audit are included. External records are regenerated outside the publication.

display.caption: Fixed-mean count score comparisons with conditional year-block intervals. The positive-count part supplies most of the primary score gain.

citations.reason: Center, window and mean design. We add a zero-inflated comparison and score decomposition. Data overlap; not independent confirmation.
